problem: Evaluating privacy vulnerabilities in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems by performing membership inference attacks to determine if specific sensitive documents are indexed in the RAG datastore (p.1-2).
methodology: The paper introduces the Interrogation Attack (IA), which uses few-shot prompting with an auxiliary LLM to generate 30 natural-text queries combining a retrieval summary and a probe question (p.2, 5-7). These benign-looking queries are submitted to the RAG system under a black-box setting, and membership is inferred by aggregating the correctness of the RAG's responses against ground-truth answers generated by a shadow LLM (p.2, 6-7).
dataset: Three scientific and medical document collections from the BEIR benchmark: NFCorpus, TREC-COVID, and SCIDOCS, containing approximately 3.5K, 116K, and 23K samples respectively (p.7).
results: The attack achieves a 2x improvement in TPR@1%FPR over prior inference attacks across diverse RAG configurations (p.1), reaching an AUC of 0.984 on Gemma-2 (2B) with the NFCorpus dataset (p.1). Straightforward detectors identify adversarial prompts from existing methods up to 76x more frequently than queries generated by the proposed attack (p.1).
key_findings: Existing RAG membership inference and extraction attacks rely on unnatural queries, jailbreaking, or prompt injection that are easily flagged by commercial detectors, whereas the proposed natural-text interrogation attack remains stealthy with detection rates as low as 5% (p.1-2, 5). Analyzing attack failure cases revealed that RAG is often unnecessary in many instances because the underlying LLM can answer questions about a given document without direct access to it (p.2).
title: Riddle Me This! Stealthy Membership Inference for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
